claim: The Drosophila melanogaster genome contains 281 putative E3 ligase-encoding genes.
source: This approach yielded 281 putative E3 ligase-encoding genes (Figure 1A), significantly higher than previously predicted for D. melanogaster (207 genes; Du et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript states that their approach identified 281 putative E3 ligase-encoding genes, which is presented as a result of their systematic search.

claim: The ratio between E3 ligase-encoding genes and total protein-coding genes is relatively constant across species at approximately 0.02-0.03.
source: The relatively constant ratio between the predicted number of E3 ligase-encoding genes and genome size across species (~0.02–0.03; Figure 1A; Ketosugbo et al., 2017), suggests an evolutionarily conserved stoichiometry between E3 ligases and target proteins, similar to protein kinases (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing the ratio across species and cites Ketosugbo et al., 2017 as supporting evidence.

claim: A core mechanism of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (protein ubiquitination) is likely conserved in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Hence, a core mechanism of the UPS – protein ubiquitination – is likely conserved in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is inferred from the conserved stoichiometry between E3 ligases and genome size across species.

claim: 157 E3 ligase-encoding genes and 11 associated genes (180 lines total) were tested in the screen.
source: After prioritizing for evolutionarily conserved genes that were shown or predicted to be expressed in the nervous system (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we investigated PHP after genetic perturbation of 157 putative E3 ligase genes and 11 associated genes (180 lines, Supplementary file 1, Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of genes and lines tested in the screen.

claim: PhTX treatment significantly reduced mEPSP amplitude in wild-type NMJs compared to untreated controls.
source: At wild-type (WT) NMJs, PhTX treatment significantly reduced mEPSP amplitude compared to untreated controls (Figure 1C, black and gray arrows), indicating GluR perturbation.
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing reduced mEPSP amplitude after PhTX treatment.

claim: AP-evoked EPSC amplitudes were similar between PhTX-treated and untreated wild-type NMJs.
source: By contrast, AP-evoked EPSC amplitudes were similar between PhTX-treated and untreated WT NMJs (Figure 1D, black and gray arrows).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing similar EPSC amplitudes.

claim: The combination of reduced mEPSP amplitude and similar EPSC amplitude suggests homeostatic increase in neurotransmitter release after PhTX treatment in wild-type, consistent with PHP.
source: Together with a reduction in mEPSP amplitude, a similar EPSC amplitude suggests a homeostatic increase in neurotransmitter release after PhTX treatment in WT, consistent with PHP (Frank et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiological data and supported by citation to Frank et al., 2006.

claim: 21 transgenic or mutant lines showed significantly smaller EPSC amplitudes compared to PhTX-treated wild-type NMJs.
source: We also identified 21 transgenic or mutant lines with significantly smaller EPSC amplitudes compared to PhTX-treated WT NMJs, and two lines with increased EPSC amplitudes (Figure 1D, E, red data).
evidence: The manuscript presents screening data identifying lines with altered EPSC amplitudes.

claim: Two transgenic or mutant lines showed increased EPSC amplitudes compared to PhTX-treated wild-type NMJs.
source: We also identified 21 transgenic or mutant lines with significantly smaller EPSC amplitudes compared to PhTX-treated WT NMJs, and two lines with increased EPSC amplitudes (Figure 1D, E, red data).
evidence: The manuscript presents screening data identifying lines with altered EPSC amplitudes.

claim: The thinΔA deletion mutant was one of the lines with significantly smaller EPSC amplitudes in the presence of PhTX.
source: One of the mutant lines with significantly smaller EPSC amplitudes in the presence of PhTX was a previously described deletion of the gene thin/abba (tn, CG15105), henceforth called thin (thinΔA; LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012; Figure 1E, filled red data).
evidence: The manuscript identifies thinΔA as a hit from the screen with supporting data in Figure 1E.

claim: thin encodes an E3 ligase with a N-terminal tripartite motif (TRIM) containing one RING-finger domain, two zinc-finger domains (B1 box and B2 box), and its associated coiled-coil region, followed by a disordered region and C-terminal NHL repeats.
source: thin encodes an E3 ligase with a N-terminal tripartite motif (TRIM), which contains one RING-finger domain, two zinc-finger domains (B1 box and B2 box), and its associated coiled-coil region, followed by a disordered region and C-terminal NHL repeats (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the domain structure of Thin based on sequence analysis.

claim: thin likely represents the Drosophila ortholog of human TRIM32.
source: Based on this domain composition, thin likely represents the Drosophila ortholog of human TRIM32 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), consistent with earlier work (LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from domain composition analysis and supported by citation to LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012.

claim: PhTX application significantly reduced mEPSC amplitude by approximately 40% in thinΔA mutants.
source: Similar to WT controls, PhTX application significantly reduced mEPSC amplitude by ~40% in thinΔA mutants (Figure 2A, B), suggesting similar receptor impairment.
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing reduced mEPSC amplitude in thinΔA mutants after PhTX treatment.

claim: At wild-type synapses, EPSC amplitudes were similar in the absence and presence of PhTX.
source: At WT synapses, EPSC amplitudes were similar in the absence and presence of PhTX (Figure 2A, C).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing similar EPSC amplitudes in WT with and without PhTX.

claim: PhTX incubation increased quantal content in wild-type, indicating homeostatic release potentiation.
source: In combination with the decrease in mEPSC amplitude (Figure 2B), PhTX incubation increased quantal content (EPSC amplitude/mEPSC amplitude) in WT (Figure 2D), indicating homeostatic release potentiation.
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing increased quantal content in WT after PhTX treatment.

claim: PhTX treatment significantly reduced EPSC amplitudes in thinΔA mutants.
source: By contrast, PhTX treatment significantly reduced EPSC amplitudes in thinΔA mutants (Figure 2A, C) and did not increase quantal content (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing reduced EPSC amplitudes in thinΔA mutants after PhTX treatment.

claim: PhTX treatment did not increase quantal content in thinΔA mutants.
source: By contrast, PhTX treatment significantly reduced EPSC amplitudes in thinΔA mutants (Figure 2A, C) and did not increase quantal content (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing no increase in quantal content in thinΔA mutants after PhTX treatment.

claim: thin is required for acute PHP expression.
source: These data show that thin is required for acute PHP expression.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the electrophysiological data showing impaired PHP in thinΔA mutants.

claim: PhTX treatment significantly reduced mEPSC amplitudes after presynaptic thin expression in the thinΔA mutant background.
source: PhTX treatment significantly reduced mEPSC amplitudes after neural/presynaptic (elavc155-Gal4) or postsynaptic (24B-Gal4) expression of thin (UAS-thin) in thinΔA mutants (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing reduced mEPSC amplitudes after presynaptic thin rescue.

claim: PhTX treatment significantly reduced mEPSC amplitudes after postsynaptic thin expression in the thinΔA mutant background.
source: PhTX treatment significantly reduced mEPSC amplitudes after neural/presynaptic (elavc155-Gal4) or postsynaptic (24B-Gal4) expression of thin (UAS-thin) in thinΔA mutants (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing reduced mEPSC amplitudes after postsynaptic thin rescue.

claim: After presynaptic thin expression in thinΔA mutants, quantal content was significantly increased upon PhTX treatment.
source: After presynaptic thin expression in thinΔA mutants (presynaptic rescue or 'pre. rescue'), quantal content was significantly increased upon PhTX treatment (Figure 2D, blue data), and EPSC amplitudes were restored toward control levels in the absence of PhTX (Figure 2A, C, blue data).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing increased quantal content after presynaptic thin rescue.

claim: After presynaptic thin expression in thinΔA mutants, EPSC amplitudes were restored toward control levels in the absence of PhTX.
source: After presynaptic thin expression in thinΔA mutants (presynaptic rescue or 'pre. rescue'), quantal content was significantly increased upon PhTX treatment (Figure 2D, blue data), and EPSC amplitudes were restored toward control levels in the absence of PhTX (Figure 2A, C, blue data).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing restored EPSC amplitudes after presynaptic thin rescue.

claim: Quantal content was similar between PhTX-treated and untreated NMJs after postsynaptic thin expression in the thinΔA mutant background.
source: By contrast, quantal content was similar between PhTX-treated and untreated NMJs after postynaptic thin expression in the thinΔA mutant background (postsynaptic rescue or 'post. rescue'; Figure 2D, green data), and PhTX application reduced EPSC amplitudes (Figure 2A, C, green data).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing no change in quantal content after postsynaptic thin rescue.

claim: PhTX application reduced EPSC amplitudes after postsynaptic thin expression in the thinΔA mutant background.
source: By contrast, quantal content was similar between PhTX-treated and untreated NMJs after postynaptic thin expression in the thinΔA mutant background (postsynaptic rescue or 'post. rescue'; Figure 2D, green data), and PhTX application reduced EPSC amplitudes (Figure 2A, C, green data).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing reduced EPSC amplitudes after postsynaptic thin rescue.

claim: Presynaptic, but not postsynaptic thin expression enhanced quantal content after PhTX treatment in the thinΔA mutant background, implying a presynaptic role for thin in PHP.
source: Thus, presynaptic, but not postsynaptic thin expression enhanced quantal content after PhTX treatment in the thinΔA mutant background (Figure 2D), implying a presynaptic role for thin in PHP.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the rescue experiments showing compartment-specific effects.

claim: thinΔA mutants displayed a decrease in mEPSC amplitude compared to wild-type in the absence of PhTX.
source: We also noted a decrease in mEPSC amplitude in thinΔA mutants compared to WT in the absence of PhTX (Figure 2A, B), which is most likely due to impaired muscle architecture in thinΔA mutants (LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012; Domsch et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing decreased mEPSC amplitude in thinΔA mutants.

claim: The decrease in mEPSC amplitude in thinΔA mutants is most likely due to impaired muscle architecture.
source: We also noted a decrease in mEPSC amplitude in thinΔA mutants compared to WT in the absence of PhTX (Figure 2A, B), which is most likely due to impaired muscle architecture in thinΔA mutants (LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012; Domsch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Postsynaptic, but not presynaptic thin expression, significantly increased mEPSC amplitudes toward wild-type levels in the thinΔA mutant background.
source: Postsynaptic, but not presynaptic thin expression, significantly increased mEPSC amplitudes toward WT levels in the thinΔA mutant background (Figure 2A, B), suggesting that postsynaptic thin is required for normal mEPSC amplitude levels.
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing compartment-specific rescue of mEPSC amplitude.

claim: Postsynaptic thin is required for normal mEPSC amplitude levels.
source: Postsynaptic, but not presynaptic thin expression, significantly increased mEPSC amplitudes toward WT levels in the thinΔA mutant background (Figure 2A, B), suggesting that postsynaptic thin is required for normal mEPSC amplitude levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing postsynaptic-specific effects on mEPSC amplitude.

claim: thinΔA mutants displayed a significant increase in quantal content compared to wild-type under baseline conditions in the absence of PhTX.
source: Furthermore, thinΔA mutants displayed a significant increase in quantal content compared to WT under baseline conditions in the absence of PhTX (Figure 2E), which was rescued by presynaptic, but not postsynaptic thin expression (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing increased quantal content in thinΔA mutants under baseline conditions.

claim: The increase in quantal content under baseline conditions in thinΔA mutants was rescued by presynaptic, but not postsynaptic thin expression.
source: Furthermore, thinΔA mutants displayed a significant increase in quantal content compared to WT under baseline conditions in the absence of PhTX (Figure 2E), which was rescued by presynaptic, but not postsynaptic thin expression (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing compartment-specific rescue of baseline quantal content.

claim: Presynaptic thin represses release under baseline conditions.
source: These data are consistent with the idea that presynaptic thin represses release under baseline conditions (see Figure 4, Figure 6).
evidence: This is inferred from the increased quantal content in thinΔA mutants and its presynaptic rescue.

claim: Genetic ablation of the GluRIIA subunit in GluRIIASP16 mutants reduces quantal size and induces sustained PHP.
source: At the Drosophila NMJ, genetic ablation of the GluRIIA subunit in GluRIIASP16 mutants reduces quantal size and induces sustained PHP (Petersen et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation to Petersen et al., 1997.

claim: A significant increase in quantal content was observed in GluRIIASP16 mutants compared to wild-type.
source: While we observed a significant increase in quantal content in GluRIIASP16 mutants compared to wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating sustained PHP expression, there was no increase in quantal content in GluRIIASP16, thinΔA double mutants compared to thinΔA mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing increased quantal content in GluRIIASP16 mutants.

claim: There was no increase in quantal content in GluRIIASP16, thinΔA double mutants compared to thinΔA mutants.
source: While we observed a significant increase in quantal content in GluRIIASP16 mutants compared to wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating sustained PHP expression, there was no increase in quantal content in GluRIIASP16, thinΔA double mutants compared to thinΔA mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing no increase in quantal content in double mutants.

claim: thin is necessary for sustained PHP expression.
source: Hence, thin is also necessary for sustained PHP expression, providing independent evidence for its role in homeostatic release regulation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the double mutant analysis showing no PHP in GluRIIASP16, thinΔA mutants.

claim: HRP area was unchanged in thinΔA mutants compared to wild-type.
source: Immunostainings with an antibody detecting neuronal membrane (anti-horseradish peroxidase, 'HRP'; Figure 3A; Jan and Jan, 1982) revealed no changes in HRP area in thinΔA mutants or after presynaptic rescue (thinΔA; elavc155-Gal4>UAS thin), and a trend toward increased HRP area after postsynaptic rescue (thinΔA; 24BGal4>UAS thin) compared to WT (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents morphological data showing no change in HRP area in thinΔA mutants.

claim: HRP area was unchanged after presynaptic rescue compared to wild-type.
source: Immunostainings with an antibody detecting neuronal membrane (anti-horseradish peroxidase, 'HRP'; Figure 3A; Jan and Jan, 1982) revealed no changes in HRP area in thinΔA mutants or after presynaptic rescue (thinΔA; elavc155-Gal4>UAS thin), and a trend toward increased HRP area after postsynaptic rescue (thinΔA; 24BGal4>UAS thin) compared to WT (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents morphological data showing no change in HRP area after presynaptic rescue.

claim: There was a trend toward increased HRP area after postsynaptic rescue compared to wild-type.
source: Immunostainings with an antibody detecting neuronal membrane (anti-horseradish peroxidase, 'HRP'; Figure 3A; Jan and Jan, 1982) revealed no changes in HRP area in thinΔA mutants or after presynaptic rescue (thinΔA; elavc155-Gal4>UAS thin), and a trend toward increased HRP area after postsynaptic rescue (thinΔA; 24BGal4>UAS thin) compared to WT (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents morphological data showing a trend toward increased HRP area after postsynaptic rescue.

claim: Brp puncta number per NMJ was unchanged in thinΔA mutants compared to wild-type.
source: Analysis of the active-zone marker Bruchpilot (anti-Bruchpilot, 'Brp'; Kittel et al., 2006) uncovered no changes in Brp puncta number per NMJ in thinΔA mutants or after presynaptic rescue, and a slight increase after postsynaptic rescue compared to WT (Figure 3A, C).
evidence: The manuscript presents morphological data showing no change in Brp puncta number in thinΔA mutants.

claim: Brp puncta number per NMJ was unchanged after presynaptic rescue compared to wild-type.
source: Analysis of the active-zone marker Bruchpilot (anti-Bruchpilot, 'Brp'; Kittel et al., 2006) uncovered no changes in Brp puncta number per NMJ in thinΔA mutants or after presynaptic rescue, and a slight increase after postsynaptic rescue compared to WT (Figure 3A, C).
evidence: The manuscript presents morphological data showing no change in Brp puncta number after presynaptic rescue.

claim: There was a slight increase in Brp puncta number after postsynaptic rescue compared to wild-type.
source: Analysis of the active-zone marker Bruchpilot (anti-Bruchpilot, 'Brp'; Kittel et al., 2006) uncovered no changes in Brp puncta number per NMJ in thinΔA mutants or after presynaptic rescue, and a slight increase after postsynaptic rescue compared to WT (Figure 3A, C).
evidence: The manuscript presents morphological data showing a slight increase in Brp puncta number after postsynaptic rescue.

claim: Brp density was unchanged in thinΔA mutants compared to wild-type.
source: Brp density (Brp puncta #/HRP area) was unchanged in thinΔA mutants or after postsynaptic rescue, and slightly increased after presynaptic rescue (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript presents morphological data showing no change in Brp density in thinΔA mutants.

claim: Brp density was unchanged after postsynaptic rescue compared to wild-type.
source: Brp density (Brp puncta #/HRP area) was unchanged in thinΔA mutants or after postsynaptic rescue, and slightly increased after presynaptic rescue (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript presents morphological data showing no change in Brp density after postsynaptic rescue.

claim: Brp density was slightly increased after presynaptic rescue compared to wild-type.
source: Brp density (Brp puncta #/HRP area) was unchanged in thinΔA mutants or after postsynaptic rescue, and slightly increased after presynaptic rescue (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript presents morphological data showing a slight increase in Brp density after presynaptic rescue.

claim: A decrease in Brp puncta intensity was observed in thinΔA mutants.
source: Finally, we observed a decrease in Brp puncta intensity in thinΔA mutants and upon presynaptic rescue (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript presents morphological data showing decreased Brp puncta intensity in thinΔA mutants.

claim: A decrease in Brp puncta intensity was observed upon presynaptic rescue.
source: Finally, we observed a decrease in Brp puncta intensity in thinΔA mutants and upon presynaptic rescue (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript presents morphological data showing decreased Brp puncta intensity after presynaptic rescue.

claim: The morphological changes seen after thin perturbation are separable from synaptic physiology.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that the morphological changes seen after thin perturbation are separable from synaptic physiology.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing morphological and physiological data across different genotypes.

claim: Changes in NMJ morphology are unlikely to underlie the defects in synaptic physiology after presynaptic loss of thin.
source: Thus, although we cannot rule out that changes in NMJ morphology contribute to the PHP defect or the increase in release in thin mutants, we consider this possibility unlikely (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the dissociation between morphological and physiological changes across genotypes.

claim: TRIM32 ubiquitinates Dysbindin and targets it for degradation in cultured human cells.
source: TRIM32, Thin's predicted human ortholog (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), ubiquitinates Dysbindin and targets it for degradation in cultured human cells (Locke et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation to Locke et al., 2009.

claim: dysbindin is required for PHP at the Drosophila NMJ.
source: dysbindin, in turn, is required for PHP at the Drosophila NMJ (Dickman and Davis, 2009), and genetic evidence suggests that the UPS controls Dysbindin under baseline conditions and during PHP at the Drosophila NMJ (Wentzel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation to Dickman and Davis, 2009.

claim: Genetic evidence suggests that the UPS controls Dysbindin under baseline conditions and during PHP at the Drosophila NMJ.
source: dysbindin, in turn, is required for PHP at the Drosophila NMJ (Dickman and Davis, 2009), and genetic evidence suggests that the UPS controls Dysbindin under baseline conditions and during PHP at the Drosophila NMJ (Wentzel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation to Wentzel et al., 2018.

claim: Presynaptic expression of fluorescently tagged dysbindin revealed that Dysbindin localizes in close proximity to synaptic vesicle markers.
source: However, presynaptic expression of a fluorescently tagged dysbindin transgene revealed that Dysbindin localizes in close proximity to synaptic vesicle markers (Dickman and Davis, 2009; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopy data showing Dysbindin localization and cites Dickman and Davis, 2009.

claim: The localization of fluorescently tagged Dysbindin likely overlaps with the one of endogenous Dysbindin, as its presynaptic expression rescues the PHP defect in dysbindin mutants.
source: The localization of fluorescently tagged Dysbindin likely overlaps with the one of endogenous Dysbindin, as its presynaptic expression rescues the PHP defect in dysbindin mutants (Dickman and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the functional rescue data and supported by citation to Dickman and Davis, 2009.

claim: Anti-Thin fluorescence was observed in close proximity to Brp.
source: Although we observed anti-Thin fluorescence in close proximity to Brp (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E), thin expression in Drosophila muscles makes it difficult to distinguish between presynaptic and postsynaptic Thin (LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopy data showing Thin localization near Brp.

claim: thin expression in Drosophila muscles makes it difficult to distinguish between presynaptic and postsynaptic Thin.
source: Although we observed anti-Thin fluorescence in close proximity to Brp (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E), thin expression in Drosophila muscles makes it difficult to distinguish between presynaptic and postsynaptic Thin (LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and supported by citation to LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012.

claim: Presynaptic ThinmCherry partially overlapped with presynaptic fluorescently tagged Dysbindin at confocal resolution.
source: Presynaptic ThinmCherry partially overlapped with presynaptic fluorescently tagged Dysbindin (elavc155-Gal4>UAS-dysbvenus) at confocal resolution (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy data showing partial overlap between ThinmCherry and Dysbindinvenus.

claim: The localization of fluorescently tagged Thin likely overlaps with endogenous Thin, because presynaptic thin expression restores PHP and synaptic transmission in thin mutants.
source: The localization of fluorescently tagged Thin also likely overlaps with endogenous Thin, because presynaptic thin expression restores PHP and synaptic transmission in thin mutants (Figure 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the functional rescue data.

claim: Dysbindin and Thin fluorescence intensity increased toward the bouton periphery.
source: As indicated by the line profile across a bouton (Figure 5B), Dysbindin and Thin fluorescence intensity increased toward the bouton periphery (Figure 5B), similar to synaptic vesicle markers, such as synapsin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopy data showing fluorescence intensity profiles.

claim: Fluorescently tagged Thin and Dysbindin appeared as distinct spots with gSTED microscopy.
source: With stimulated emission depletion microscopy with time-gated detection (gSTED), fluorescently tagged Thin and Dysbindin appeared as distinct spots (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript presents gSTED microscopy data showing distinct spots.

claim: Nearest-neighbor distances between ThinmCherry and Dysbvenus spots were significantly smaller than expected from random spot distributions.
source: This analysis revealed significantly smaller NNDs between ThinmCherry and Dysbvenus spots than expected from random spot distributions (Figure 5E), implying a relationship between Thin and Dysbindin localization within synaptic boutons.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative analysis of NND data compared to simulated random distributions.

claim: The NND analysis implies a relationship between Thin and Dysbindin localization within synaptic boutons.
source: This analysis revealed significantly smaller NNDs between ThinmCherry and Dysbvenus spots than expected from random spot distributions (Figure 5E), implying a relationship between Thin and Dysbindin localization within synaptic boutons.
evidence: This is inferred from the NND analysis showing non-random spatial relationships.

claim: A fraction of Thin localizes in the vicinity of Dysbindin and synaptic vesicles.
source: Based on the proximity between Dysbindin and synaptic vesicle markers (Dickman and Davis, 2009; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C), these data indicate that a fraction of Thin localizes in the vicinity of Dysbindin and synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data and supported by citation to Dickman and Davis, 2009.

claim: Anti-Thin fluorescence was homogenously distributed within S2 cells under control conditions.
source: Interestingly, while anti-Thin fluorescence was homogenously distributed within S2 cells under control conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), dysbindin (dysbvenus) overexpression led to a redistribution of anti-Thin fluorescence into clusters that localized in close proximity to anti-Dysbindin clusters (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopy data from S2 cells showing Thin distribution under control conditions.

claim: dysbindin overexpression led to a redistribution of anti-Thin fluorescence into clusters that localized in close proximity to anti-Dysbindin clusters in S2 cells.
source: Interestingly, while anti-Thin fluorescence was homogenously distributed within S2 cells under control conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), dysbindin (dysbvenus) overexpression led to a redistribution of anti-Thin fluorescence into clusters that localized in close proximity to anti-Dysbindin clusters (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopy data from S2 cells showing Thin redistribution upon dysbindin overexpression.

claim: Anti-Thin and anti-Dysbindin fluorescence intensities were highly correlated in S2 cells overexpressing dysbindin.
source: Moreover, anti-Thin and anti-Dysbindin fluorescence intensities were highly correlated (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), suggesting a possible interaction between Thin and Dysbindin in S2 cells, similar to the Drosophila NMJ (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript presents correlation analysis of fluorescence intensities in S2 cells.

claim: The high correlation between anti-Thin and anti-Dysbindin fluorescence intensities suggests a possible interaction between Thin and Dysbindin in S2 cells.
source: Moreover, anti-Thin and anti-Dysbindin fluorescence intensities were highly correlated (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), suggesting a possible interaction between Thin and Dysbindin in S2 cells, similar to the Drosophila NMJ (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation analysis.

claim: A decrease in Dysbvenus levels was observed upon increasing ThinHA expression levels in S2 cells.
source: We observed a decrease in Dysbvenus levels upon increasing ThinHA expression levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: The manuscript presents western blot data showing decreased Dysbindin levels with increased Thin expression.

claim: The data are consistent with the idea that Thin acts as an E3 ligase for Dysbindin in Drosophila, similar to TRIM32 in humans.
source: Although we cannot exclude the possibility that Thin overexpression induced artificial Dysbindin ubiquitination by excess enzyme binding with low affinity, these data are consistent with the idea that Thin acts as an E3 ligase for Dysbindin in Drosophila, similar to TRIM32 in humans (Locke et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the biochemical data and supported by citation to Locke et al., 2009.

claim: Presynaptic thinRNAi expression in the wild-type background did not affect mEPSC amplitude.
source: Neither presynaptic thinRNAi expression (elavc155-Gal4>UAS-thinRNAi) in the WT background, nor in the dysb1 mutant background affected mEPSC amplitude (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing no change in mEPSC amplitude after presynaptic thinRNAi in WT.

claim: Presynaptic thinRNAi expression in the dysb1 mutant background did not affect mEPSC amplitude.
source: Neither presynaptic thinRNAi expression (elavc155-Gal4>UAS-thinRNAi) in the WT background, nor in the dysb1 mutant background affected mEPSC amplitude (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing no change in mEPSC amplitude after presynaptic thinRNAi in dysb1 mutants.

claim: Presynaptic thinRNAi expression enhanced EPSC amplitude and quantal content in the wild-type background.
source: While presynaptic thinRNAi expression enhanced EPSC amplitude and quantal content in the WT background (Figure 6C, D; see also Figure 4), presynaptic thinRNAi expression neither affected EPSC amplitude (Figure 6C) nor quantal content (Figure 6D) in the dysb1 mutant background.
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing enhanced EPSC amplitude and quantal content after presynaptic thinRNAi in WT.

claim: Presynaptic thinRNAi expression did not affect EPSC amplitude in the dysb1 mutant background.
source: While presynaptic thinRNAi expression enhanced EPSC amplitude and quantal content in the WT background (Figure 6C, D; see also Figure 4), presynaptic thinRNAi expression neither affected EPSC amplitude (Figure 6C) nor quantal content (Figure 6D) in the dysb1 mutant background.
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing no change in EPSC amplitude after presynaptic thinRNAi in dysb1 mutants.

claim: Presynaptic thinRNAi expression did not affect quantal content in the dysb1 mutant background.
source: While presynaptic thinRNAi expression enhanced EPSC amplitude and quantal content in the WT background (Figure 6C, D; see also Figure 4), presynaptic thinRNAi expression neither affected EPSC amplitude (Figure 6C) nor quantal content (Figure 6D) in the dysb1 mutant background.
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing no change in quantal content after presynaptic thinRNAi in dysb1 mutants.

claim: The genetic data provide evidence that thin negatively controls release through dysbindin.
source: These data provide genetic evidence that thin negatively controls release through dysbindin (Figure 6E).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the epistasis analysis showing that dysbindin is required for thin's effect on release.

claim: The study represents the first systematic investigation of E3 ligase function in the context of synaptic transmission.
source: Our study represents the first systematic investigation of E3 ligase function in the context of synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: 11% of the transgenic lines tested displayed a decrease in EPSC amplitude after PhTX treatment.
source: A considerable fraction of the transgenic lines tested (11%) displayed a decrease in EPSC amplitude after PhTX treatment (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: The manuscript presents screening data showing the percentage of lines with decreased EPSC amplitude.

claim: Previous PHP screens in the same system identified PHP mutants with a hit rate of approximately 3%.
source: Previous PHP screens in the same system identified PHP mutants with a hit rate of ~3% (Dickman and Davis, 2009; Müller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The data indicate that E3 ligase function plays a special role in PHP and/or baseline synaptic transmission.
source: Thus, our data indicate that E3 ligase function plays a special role in PHP and/or baseline synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the hit rate in this screen to previous screens.

claim: The net effect of E3 ligases is to promote synaptic transmission at the Drosophila NMJ.
source: As more transgenic or mutant lines exhibited a decrease in synaptic transmission, we conclude that the net effect of E3 ligases is to promote synaptic transmission at the Drosophila NMJ.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the screening data showing more lines with decreased transmission.

claim: The E3 ligase highwire restrains synaptic growth and promotes evoked synaptic transmission at the Drosophila NMJ.
source: For instance, the E3 ligase highwire (hiw) restrains synaptic growth and promotes evoked synaptic transmission at the Drosophila NMJ (Wan et al., 2000).
